definition: In the field of mathematical optimization, stochastic programming is a framework for modeling optimization problems that involve uncertainty.
details: A stochastic program is an optimization problem in which some or all problem parameters are uncertain, but follow known probability distributions. This framework contrasts with deterministic optimization, in which all problem parameters are assumed to be known exactly. The goal of stochastic programming is to find a decision which both optimizes some criteria chosen by the decision maker, and appropriately accounts for the uncertainty of the problem parameters. Because many real-world decisions involve uncertainty, stochastic programming has found applications in a broad range of areas ranging from finance to transportation to energy optimization.

explainer.lead: A mathematical-optimization framework for problems where some or all parameters are uncertain but follow known probability distributions. It matters because most real-world decisions are made without exact knowledge of their parameters.

tiers.eli5: Planning when some numbers are unknown, but you know the odds — you choose a plan that does well on average rather than betting on one guess.
tiers.practitioner: Used where uncertainty can be characterised probabilistically, e.g. planning under demand or price uncertainty; the pitfall is that misspecified distributions silently bias the chosen decision.
tiers.paperLevel: An optimization problem in which some or all problem parameters are uncertain but follow known probability distributions, contrasting with deterministic optimization where all parameters are assumed known exactly; the goal is a decision that optimizes a chosen criterion while accounting for parameter uncertainty.

explainer.example: Choosing production levels when demand follows a known distribution, rather than assuming a single fixed demand figure.
